title: Self-sovereign identity
lede: A Nostr keypair replaces email, password, and platform account. No custodian. Recovery is a 12-word seed.
what: Nostr (Notes on a Public Message Network) uses public-key cryptography instead of usernames. Each user gets a keypair: a public key (npub) they share, and a private key (nsec) they keep. The private key signs every action. Lose the key and you lose the identity — so a 12-word seed phrase is the recovery mechanism.
why: Caribbean apps built on platform accounts inherit the platform's risk: a payment processor deplatforms them, a regional bank cuts off the KYC vendor, a hosting provider exits. Nostr keys are interoperable with hundreds of apps and don't depend on any single company.

title: Lightning payment rail
lede: Apps call the SDK. The user signs. The app never holds funds. Works from anywhere with internet.
what: Lightning is a fast Bitcoin payment network. Invoices (BOLT11) carry a payment request. NWC (Nostr Wallet Connect, NIP-47) lets an app ask the user's wallet to pay without ever touching the private key. The wallet signs. Settlement happens on the base layer.
why: Card networks decline Caribbean merchants. Banks require a US presence. Lightning works from any internet connection, charges no merchant fee, and doesn't care about geography.

title: Federated fiat ramp
lede: Independent Mostro nodes compete on rate and fee. Caribbean rails first. No platform in the middle.
what: Mostro is a federated network of market makers. Each node publishes a profile (kind:38383) listing supported fiats, settlement methods, fees, and reputation. Wallets rank nodes per-order using a deterministic rubric. No single operator sits in the middle.
why: Onboarding fiat is the hardest problem for a Caribbean app builder. Hosted card processors don't serve them. Flutterwave has gaps. By federating the ramp, Voyager lets multiple operators compete for the trade instead of locking users into one custodian.

title: Private messaging
lede: NIP-17 gift-wrapped DMs give any app end-to-end encrypted messaging without building a Signal clone.
what: NIP-17 specifies 'gift-wrapped' direct messages. The sender encrypts to the recipient's public key, wraps that in a kind:1059 event, and publishes. Relays see opaque blobs. Only the recipient can decrypt. Order details, contract terms, addresses — none of it visible to relays.
why: Order confirmation by SMS leaks phone numbers. Email leaks metadata to a third party. Signal is great but requires building a separate identity layer. NIP-17 reuses the user's Nostr identity and lets any builder ship messaging in a few SDK calls.

title: Discovery substrate
lede: Listings, profiles, and ramp quotes as signed Nostr events. Relays and indexers handle findability.
what: Three Nostr event kinds cover most marketplace needs: kind:30402 (replaceable listings — accommodations, tours, goods), kind:30017 (stalls — a vendor's catalogue), kind:38383 (ramp quotes — federated fiat). Addressable means each (pubkey, kind, d-tag) tuple resolves to a single current value. Any relay or independent indexer can serve search.
why: Central marketplaces (Airbnb, Etsy, Amazon) own discoverability and tax it. On Nostr, every listing is a signed public event. Search is fan-out across relays. The protocol doesn't ship a search UI — that's the app's job — but it makes search a one-call SDK operation.
